The free-rider problem has long beset the National Health Service: that is, people who use the health service without paying into it, thereby leaving existing taxpayers to bear an unwarranted burden.

The proposed solution was called a freerider system because, if a driver didn't run a fast race, there would be more people in the next race and these ‘freeriders’ could benefit even though they were not actually competing.
The freeriders of the world are not only the wealthy nations but also some of those which they have given legitimacy and assistance.
If freeriders are excluded from registration, this has important implications for the relationship between free riders and their host.

These services are also open to free riders, people living within local authority areas but residing outside the boundaries of the county authority area, providing they can satisfy any required residence or waiting time requirements.
In an era of Reaganianism and individualistic ethics, the notion that a single person can work effectively alone, or as part of an unholy coalition of free riders is more common than ever.
The freerider problem is one that has always beset national health programs.

It is therefore difficult to see why people would not benefit from a world-wide government provided there are good institutions and regulations that prevent free riders from drawing a living at the expense of other nations' residents.
As long as there are people who cannot get around to working with the rest of us, there will be free riders and there will be free riders' problems.
